skill.name: event-sourcing-architect
skill.description: Design event-sourced systems with CQRS, immutable events, projections, sagas, snapshots, schema evolution, and eventual consistency.
skill.summary: Plan reliable event-sourced architectures for complex domains and auditable workflows.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: The only static finding is a false positive caused by Markdown backticks around related skill names. The skill contains architectural guidance and no executable commands or malicious instructions.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 66 uses Markdown backticks to format related skill names. It contains no Ruby code, shell command, or execution instruction.

content.value_statement: Complex domains need traceable state changes, resilient workflows, and query models built for their access patterns. This skill guides practical event sourcing and CQRS decisions.
actual_capabilities: Identifies aggregate boundaries, command flows, event streams, and immutable domain events.
Designs CQRS read models and projections around specific query requirements.
Structures sagas and process managers with retries, compensation, and correlation identifiers.
Plans snapshotting strategies for long-lived aggregates and high-volume event streams.
Defines event versioning, schema evolution, and projection rebuild approaches.
Addresses eventual consistency, idempotent handlers, audit trails, and temporal queries.
limitations: Event sourcing adds unnecessary complexity when standard CRUD satisfies the domain.
The guidance does not replace environment-specific testing, operational validation, or expert review.
Teams must be able to operate event stores, projections, and replay procedures.
The approach cannot provide immediate consistency across every distributed workflow.

use_cases.title: Model an Auditable Domain
use_cases.description: Define aggregates, commands, and events for systems that require complete state histories and temporal queries.

use_cases.title: Build CQRS Read Models
use_cases.description: Plan projections, replay behavior, and idempotent handlers for application-specific query needs.

use_cases.title: Coordinate Distributed Workflows
use_cases.description: Design sagas with durable state, retries, timeouts, and compensating actions across services.

prompt_templates.title: Map an Event-Sourced Aggregate
prompt_templates.prompt: Map an event-sourced aggregate for [domain]. Identify commands, immutable events, aggregate boundaries, and one read model. Explain each choice.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this for a first event sourcing design.

prompt_templates.title: Design a CQRS Architecture
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a CQRS architecture for [system]. Define write flows, event streams, projections, consistency expectations, idempotency controls, and failure handling.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this when separating command and query workloads.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Distributed Saga
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a saga for [workflow] across [services]. Include steps, correlation identifiers, retries, timeouts, compensating actions, and observable failure states.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this for workflows spanning several aggregates or services.

prompt_templates.title: Review an Evolving Event System
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this architecture: [details]. Propose event versioning, upcasting, snapshotting, projection rebuilds, temporal queries, disaster recovery, and a staged validation plan.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this for mature systems with schema and performance concerns.

output_examples.input: Design an event-sourced order aggregate with cancellation support.
output_examples.output: The Order aggregate records placement, item changes, confirmation, and cancellation as facts. Cancellation rules depend on prior events and publish projection updates.

output_examples.input: Plan payment and inventory coordination for checkout.
output_examples.output: A checkout saga correlates reservations and payment authorization. It retries transient failures, times out stalled steps, and compensates completed reservations after terminal failures.

output_examples.input: Prepare a versioning plan for an existing customer event.
output_examples.output: Keep committed events immutable. Introduce a new version, define deterministic upcasting, rebuild projections in staging, and compare results before production rollout.

best_practices: Model events as immutable business facts with stable identifiers and clear ownership.
Make handlers idempotent and propagate correlation identifiers through every workflow step.
Test projection rebuilds, schema changes, and recovery procedures before production use.
anti_patterns: Do not mutate or delete committed production events to correct business state.
Do not introduce event sourcing when simple transactional CRUD meets the requirements.
Do not let projections become authoritative write models or hide consistency expectations.

faq.question: When should I choose event sourcing?
faq.answer: Choose it when the domain needs audit history, temporal queries, complex state transitions, or durable workflow coordination.

faq.question: Does this skill generate production code?
faq.answer: It primarily provides architecture guidance and design artifacts. Any generated implementation still requires testing, review, and adaptation to your environment.

faq.question: Can it design CQRS projections?
faq.answer: Yes. It can map query requirements to read models, projection handlers, replay behavior, and consistency expectations.

faq.question: How does it address event schema changes?
faq.answer: It can propose versioned events, deterministic upcasting, compatibility rules, and staged projection rebuilds.

faq.question: Can it help with distributed transactions?
faq.answer: It can design sagas and process managers using retries, timeouts, durable state, and compensating actions.

faq.question: What information should I provide?
faq.answer: Provide domain rules, consistency needs, query patterns, expected volume, service boundaries, failure cases, and operational constraints.
